title: Placement and Lease-based Routing — sketch
content:
Quick sketch / working notes about using a lease-based placement and routing layer for control-plane resources.

  Context and goal
  - Problem: control-plane CRUD operations (create/update/delete) need a deterministic target for writes and fast consistent reads across regions without creating huge operational coupling.
  - Goal: a small, explicit placement system so API servers (control plane frontends) can route writes to a stable primary for a resource (or short-lived owner set), and reads can be served from local caches/secondaries with bounded staleness guarantees.
  - We prefer a lightweight approach (leases + heartbeats + optional cross-region write fanout) instead of full-blown distributed consensus for every object.

  Design sketch: placement lease model
  - Each named resource (resource-id) can be assigned a placement record:
    - owner: cluster-id (or an affinity set of clusters for multi-primary allowed cases)
    - lease_id: opaque token
    - lease_expires_at: monotonic timestamp
    - generation: monotonic int incremented on ownership change
    - routing_hints: {preferred-region, fallback-regions, read_ttl_secs}
  - Lease lifecycle:
    - Acquire: cluster writes a new placement with a conditional create (if generation matches expected) and receives lease_id.
    - Renew: owner sends heartbeat update before lease_expires_at to extend the lease (idempotent renew using lease_id).
    - Release: owner explicitly drops lease (set owner=null, generation++).
    - Expire: control-plane detects missing heartbeats; a background reconciler can mark expired and allow re-acquire.
  - Short leases (30s–120s) allow quick failover but increase churn. Pick defaults by workload class.

  API semantics (control-plane CRUD layer)
  - Write path options (configurable per resource type):
    1) Direct routed write: API frontend resolves placement and proxies the write to owner cluster (preferred for strong write locality).
    2) Orchestrated fanout: frontend accepts a write and orchestrates a fanout to owner(s) asynchronously with transactional hints (useful for multi-cluster replication).
    3) Fallback-local-commit: frontend writes to a fast local staging store and then forwards to owner; used where frontend must remain responsive under owner unavailability.

  - Read semantics:
    - By default, reads are served from regional caches with read_ttl configured in placement record. If caller requests strong read-after-write, the frontend can route to owner for an up-to-date read (or do a conditional read with generation check).
    - Provide an explicit query param ?consistency=strict|bounded|stale to let clients indicate expectations.

  Idempotency and conflict handling
  - All mutating CRUD endpoints must accept an idempotency_key header. If request retry arrives, owner should deduplicate using that key.
  - For cross-region write fanout we keep a small write-log entry (log_id) per write; consumer clusters apply in sequence using generation and conditional checks.
  - Conflicts (concurrent updates) resolved by generation-based compare-and-set; if application-level merges are needed, surface conflict to client with a 409 and provide a minimal merge helper route.

  Failure modes and observability
  - Owner unresponsive => lease expiry => reconciler tries to select a new owner. During handover, API frontends should return 503 for strict writes or route to fallback mode if configured.
  - Split-brain risk: lease race could result in two clusters thinking they own resource if clock skew / reconciliation bug. Mitigations:
    - Use monotonic logical generation bumps with ownership proofs (lease_id + signed attestations) for safer handoff.
    - Reconciler must use last-writer-wins with generation and prefer non-expired heartbeats.
  - Metrics to emit:
    - lease_acquire_attempts, lease_renew_rate, lease_expiry_count
    - routed_write_latency_by_cluster, read_staleness_histogram
    - routing_failover_count, fanout_retry_count

  Operational patterns
  - Resource typing: not every resource needs dynamic placement. Classify resource kinds:
    - Global-singleton (e.g., org-level metadata) => strong placement, conservative short leases, owner in control-plane region.
    - Tenant-scoped high-throughput (e.g., inference-config) => prefer colocated cluster in tenant's region, allow bounded stale reads.
    - Ephemeral resources (jobs, one-offs) => can be leaderless; rely on idempotency keys and best-effort routing.

  - Placement reconciliation loop:
    - Periodic scan (N hours) to ensure placement records map to live clusters. Remove orphans, log audit.
    - React to cluster decommission events: mark affected placement leases expired immediately, kick reconciliation.

  Lightweight protocols and storage
  - Where to store placement records? Options:
    - Central durable store (single control-plane DB) — simplest but centralizes routing.
    - Sharded placement service (per-region control-plane with cross-region replication) — reduces latency for resolution.
    - Use a compact KV (etcd-like) if we want watch-based invalidations for frontends.

  - Frontend resolution cache:
    - Frontends cache placement records per resource-id with TTL equal to min(read_ttl, lease_expires_at - now, 5s). On cache miss or near-expiry, fetch placement service with conditional-if-changed.

  Handoff and step-down choreography
  - When owner intentionally steps down, sequence:
    1) Owner sets state=draining with routing_hints (delay writes) and stops accepting new work
    2) Owner waits for in-flight ops flush, optionally hands off outstanding leases (transfer with generation bump)
    3) Owner issues release (owner=null or new-owner set) and increments generation
    4) Reconciler verifies and marks transition complete

  Debugging tips for oncall
  - Quick checks:
    - placement record for resource: show owner, lease_id, expires_at, generation
    - recent heartbeat times and renewal failures
    - fanout logs for pending writes
  - Useful CLI: rctl placement get <resource-id> --verbose, rctl placement transfer <resource-id> --target-cluster=<id>

  Open questions / trade-offs
  - Lease duration tuning: shorter => faster recovery, more churn; longer => lower overhead, riskier failover. Consider per-resource defaults.
  - Strong consistency mode: do we ever require single-region serializability? If yes, might need a quorum or leader-election with persistent consensus for those resource classes.
  - Cross-region write amplification: can we allow a write path that accepts writes in any region and uses causal logs to reconcile? That increases complexity.
  - Placement storage single-point-of-failure: Consider multi-active placement services with leaderless reads and conflict resolution.

  Next steps / proposed experiment
  - Implement a placement-service prototype backing onto an existing control-plane DB table + short TTL cache in frontends.
  - Run a synthetic test: 10k resource IDs, lease 60s, simulate owner failures, measure failover median latency and number of split-brain events under clock skew injection.
  - Draft simple API contract for frontends and owners (AcquireLease, RenewLease, ReleaseLease, GetPlacement, ListStalePlacements).

  TODOs
  - [ ] Write minimal OpenAPI spec for Acquire/Renew/Release/GetPlacement (owner auth, idempotency rules).
  - [ ] Add telemetry hooks to placement flow (traces + counters).
  - [ ] Create a lightweight reconciler runbook for oncall.

  Notes to self
  - Keep this as a sketch. Will convert into a playbook if experiment shows acceptable failure modes.
  - Sync with SRE and serving-runtime teams (heartbeats/connection limits) before choosing default lease window.

  References
  - link: https://martin.kleppmann.com/notes/consensus-vs-lease
  - jira: JIRA-PLAT-743 (placement experiments)
  - pr: github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/1289
